Java: 21 LTS, pinned by toolchain
Build tool: Gradle 9.9.1, Kotlin DSL, per-module toolchains
Modules: `core`, `mcp-adapter`, `daemon`, `api`, `apiclient`, `client`, `cli`, `standalone`, `testkit`
MCP library: `io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp` 2.1.0 (MIT), `StdioServerTransportProvider`
Spring: Spring Boot 4.x in `api` and `daemon` only, no JavaFX in that JVM
Persistence: SQLite via `org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc` 3.54.1.0, WAL, `busy_timeout`, one writer thread
Tests: JUnit 5 and AssertJ for core; JavaFX headless platform for a thin UI smoke layer
Packaging: `jlink` or `jpackage` image, JavaFX always on the module path
MCP Java SDK: `io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp`, MIT, Java 17+, core ships STDIO, SSE, and Streamable HTTP server transports with no web framework
Registry `<latest>` is a milestone, so pin 2.1.0
JavaFX must load from named modules on the module path; classpath loading is documented as unsupported
`Platform.startup` is the supported way to start the toolkit from a non-JavaFX main; `Application.launch` may only be called once and not from the FX thread
Headless JavaFX: JavaFX 26 adds a headless Glass platform selected with `-Dglass.platform=headless`, with no extra artifact
SQLite WAL runs with exactly one writer at a time and does not work over a network filesystem; `busy_timeout` and `locking_mode` are the documented controls
`core` declares no Spring and no JavaFX dependency
Enforce the `core` dependency rule with a build check, or standalone mode drifts into needing Spring
Both run modes assemble from the same modules: standalone takes `core` + `mcp-adapter` + `client`; split takes `core` + `mcp-adapter` + `api` + `daemon`, `client` through `apiclient`
A Spring Boot fat jar is not a supported JavaFX host, so packaging is an image, not a single jar
A task is a flat key/value map of strings, with no required key at the storage layer
Recognized keys are a small set; every other key is a user-defined attribute
Multi-valued fields are stored one key per member (`tag_<name>`, `dep_<uuid>`, `annotation_<epoch>`) so a single modification can add or remove one member without a read-modify-write
`uuid`: permanent, non-modifiable identity
The numeric `id` is only a line number in the working set and changes, so external references must use the UUID
`status`: one of `pending`, `completed`, `deleted`, `recurring`
`waiting` is virtual, derived from a pending task whose `wait` date is in the future, and is translated back to `pending` on write
`description`: one line, required by validation, not by storage
`entry`, `modified`: creation and last-change timestamps
`start`: the most recent start time; its presence defines "active"
`start` is a single timestamp, not an interval and not a total
`end`: completion or deletion time; removed when the task is restored
`due`: deadline
`scheduled`: first opportunity to begin work; a readiness label, not a constraint
`wait`: hidden until the date passes; reaching it removes the date
`recur`, `mask`, `imask`, `parent`: recurrence template and its instances
`depends`: a set of UUIDs, one key each
`tags`: a set of words, no spaces, restricted leading characters
`annotations`: free text keyed by timestamp, add-only, no author, no ids
`project`: one string, with `.` for a naming hierarchy
`priority`: `H`, `M`, `L`, or empty; a built-in user-defined attribute
`urgency`: a float that is computed and cached in memory, never stored, and explicitly ignored on input
User-defined attributes: declared in configuration with a type of string, numeric, date, duration, or uuid, plus an optional allowed-value list, default, label, and urgency coefficient
Legal transitions: create to pending
Legal transitions: pending to completed or deleted, each setting `end`
Legal transitions: completed or deleted back to pending, clearing `end`
Legal transitions: recurring to completed at `until`
Legal transitions: deleted to gone only by `purge`, which is local, unsynced, and irreversible
Recurrence templates spawn children linked by `parent` and `imask`, and child status writes back into the template's `mask`
One SQLite database, `taskchampion.sqlite3`, in the data directory, replacing the 2.x text files
The store is transaction protected at serializable isolation
Every change becomes an operation: create, delete with the old task, update with old and new value and timestamp
An undo point marks a command boundary
Undo reverses operations back to a boundary and refuses if the sequence moved
Tasks carry no history field; the operation log is the history
Deleted and undone tasks are not tombstones in a separate file: a deleted task is a normal row with a status and an end date
Dependencies accept ids, UUIDs, and ranges
Dependencies reject self-edges, and reject cycles by traversing the pending cache
Completing or starting a blocked task prints a warning and offers to repair the chain; it does not refuse
There is no edge type and no scheduling
Tags are an unstructured word set
Annotations are immutable free text
Neither tags nor annotations can express a key and value, which is exactly why user-defined attributes exist
Urgency is a weighted polynomial over due, blocking, priority, scheduled, active, age, annotations, tags, project, waiting, and blocked, with per-tag, per-project, and per-attribute coefficients
No estimate
No time tracking: start and stop times are not time tracking
No assignment or owner
No per-day capacity, availability, or scheduling
No subtask hierarchy; `parent` means a recurrence template
No structured annotation, no edge type, no history on the task
workthread needs an estimate, logged work, remaining effort, a timetable, and a session, so it needs a model that carries numbers and time entries, not only dates and tags
Ideas worth carrying over: the flat extensible attribute set, one key per member for set-valued fields
Ideas worth carrying over: an operation log for history, a virtual derived status rather than a stored one
Ideas worth carrying over: the discipline of separating stored facts from computed ones (urgency is recomputed; it is never an input)
Yes: a JavaFX 21 client ships as a self-contained image from a Gradle build
The `--jmod` artifacts that older guides mention do not exist on Maven Central; every route consumes modular jars
Chosen direction: the `org.beryx.jlink` plugin, with `--strip-debug --compress zip-6`
The image is not fully self-contained on Linux: every image still needs the host's GTK3 and X11 libraries
The distribution constraint must be recorded in the packaging child effort's scope
Every JavaFX tray library wraps AWT
`FXTrayIcon` 4.2.3 is a thin wrapper whose module descriptor requires `java.desktop` and `javafx.swing`
Because `javafx.graphics` already requires `java.desktop`, a no-tray image saves nothing
The tray is an application decision rather than a packaging one
Chosen direction: `FXTrayIcon` guarded by `SystemTray.isSupported()`, with graceful degradation to the window when no tray exists
Unguarded construction throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and ends the application
Every `jpackage` image printed an unexplained "pure virtual method called" at startup, including a pure-JavaFX app, and the app still ran
JavaFX natives are extracted from the image and cached in `~/.openjfx/cache`, which works with a read-only home
AWT initialization inside the GTK app emits a `Gdk-WARNING` about `XSetErrorHandler`
Not verifiable here: icon appearance, native menu firing, GTK and AWT stability with a real tray, GNOME and AppIndicator behavior, HiDPI, and the deb and rpm artifacts
A real desktop test is an acceptance item for the tray child effort
Yes: one JVM can host Spring Boot and JavaFX, with an explicit shutdown order
Spring Boot owns main, starts the context, then Platform.startup: recommended when Spring is in the process
The only hard failure is the java launcher's main-class check, which fires only when the main class extends javafx.application.Application
Packaging a runnable jar makes the documented-unsupported configuration the default configuration
The Spring context does not close on Platform.exit()
Without an explicit close it is closed by Spring Boot's shutdown hook, and the hook ordering varied between runs
The shape that behaves is Variant A with an explicit order: Platform.exit() on the FX thread, then a latch, then context.close() on the main thread
--add-modules javafx.controls, or the app dies with NoClassDefFoundError: javafx/scene/Parent
-linux classified JavaFX jars, because the unclassified stubs fail with FindException: Module javafx.controls not found
The build must enforce the module path, because the runtime does not. This is a scaffolding and packaging requirement, not advice
Full evidence, the cases verbatim, the comparison table, and the rule snippets: `docs/research/prototype-ordering-engine.md`
Question answered: yes, with one criteria gap. The timetable and session model reproduce the specification's capacity arithmetic exactly...
Chosen direction, confirmed by the human: Rule A with inherited deadlines is the ordering rule
A prerequisite inherits the earliest effective deadline of the tasks it unblocks
The prototype checked the inherited-deadline arithmetic by hand and did not implement it; the scheduling child implements it
The chain day under rule A is the one the human accepted: three prerequisites in sequence, the deadline-bearing task at 11:00, and a 45 minute task due the next noon carried to Thursday
The fit signal cannot say "does not fit", so the scheduling engine needs an explicit does-not-fit state
`session-and-timetable` must name the does-not-fit state
Timetable values are net working minutes per weekday
A future forecast day starts at a fixed placeholder time
The session is a hard boundary, and a chunk never crosses the planned leave time
The five minute completion slot applies only to zero remaining effort
Dependency pressure is static least slack among the deadline-bearing descendants
Dependency depth is the count of unfinished transitive prerequisites
Yes: one CLI binary can serve MCP over stdio and stay usable interactively.
Chosen direction: A subcommand that owns standard input and output for its whole lifetime, `mcp serve`, with every other subcommand staying interactive.
Dependency: `io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp:2.1.0`, the newest non-milestone; 2.2.0-M2 exists.
The `mcp` artifact is an empty aggregator: the real code is `mcp-core` plus `mcp-json-jackson3`
Standard output purity held only because the logging backend was pinned to stderr at warn level.
Any module that can serve MCP must guarantee that nothing writes to standard out in that mode
The build should make the stderr configuration the default rather than a comment.
The SDK needs no glue. The transport's reader thread is non-daemon, so a plain serve-and-return keeps the JVM alive until standard input reaches end of file, then exits 0.
`Tool.builder()` is deprecated and the schema must be passed to the factory.
The JSON mapper must be supplied explicitly through `McpJsonDefaults.getMapper()`.
`capabilities()` and `serverInfo()` are optional but default to a generic server name and version.
The `logging` capability is always advertised with no way to disable it.
Requests sent before initialize get silence rather than an error, and pipelined requests followed by an immediate end of input drop the response tail.
Consequence for the agent interface: the tool registration shape is known and cheap.
The risk is not the SDK; it is any logging framework that defaults to standard out, which is exactly what Spring Boot does.

The capacity model no longer has availability exceptions, since per-date vacation and flex entries replaced them
It no longer has clock intervals, since a weekday is a minute count inside one local day
Removing a per-date entry is an explicit removal
A working day never crosses midnight
A task is cancelled and a project is archived; nothing is deleted on request
Configuration carries a purge age in days, off by default; when it is set, a record whose cancellation or archiving is older than that many days is permanently deleted
Nothing is ever deleted while the setting is off
The moment of cancellation or archiving is recorded as a timestamp on the record, because the age is measured from it, which adds a cancellation timestamp to a task and an archival timestamp...
Purging an archived project takes its tasks, notes, time entries, and dependencies with it, and the setting's own description says so
Every purge writes a log entry
A batch raises an ephemeral notice naming how many records went and how old they were
The purge is not an operation anyone can invoke directly; it is a scheduled consequence of the setting
Removal asks for confirmation when, and only when, it changes something already reported: a per-date entry on a past date, a closed time entry, or a note
Plan-only removals, a future date entry or a task with no history, happen at once
The operation log keeps the removed content in either case, so the confirmation is about intent rather than recoverability
The review compares each past day's target minutes with the presence recorded for it, both recomputed from current configuration at the moment it is shown
No past itinerary is stored and no past itinerary is reconstructed

`note`: the reason for `refused` and `deferred`, and anything a reader needs to follow `superseded` and `duplicate`; empty otherwise

Daemon: The process that holds the work logic and runs without a user interface.
Client: The JavaFX surface the user interacts with.
Standalone mode: An arrangement where a surface reaches the work logic in the same process, with no API between them.
Split mode: An arrangement where a surface reaches the work logic in another process, through the API.
Note: A timestamped piece of text appended to a task.
Core: The module holding the work logic: the domain model, the use cases, and the surface ports they implement.
Surface: A driving adapter that exposes the work logic to something outside the core: the command line interface, the MCP server, the client, the tray.
Surface port: An interface on the core's surface side.
Infrastructure port: An interface on the core's infrastructure side.
Adapter: A component outside the core that implements an infrastructure port: the SQLite store, the system clock, the change log writer.
Remote proxy: An implementation of the surface ports that forwards each call to the daemon over the API, so a surface can run without the core in its own process.
Timetable: The net work minutes held by each weekday, one window per weekday.
Planned start: The configured clock time at which a day is expected to begin.
Session: The record of one working day: when it was started, its leave time, and its break reserve.
Leave time: The instant a working day is planned to end, derived from the start and the day's minutes and moved at any moment during the day.
Stop time: The instant a working day actually ended, entered by the user or inferred when the day was left open.
Break reserve: Minutes set aside for breaks within a day.
Target: The minutes a month owes: the sum of its weekdays' timetable minutes, minus the minutes of vacation recorded on those dates.
Balance: Minutes of presence worked in a month minus that month's target, running inside the month and followed by the plan.
Presence: The minutes between a session's start and its stop time, minus the break reserve.
Vacation: A per-date entry that reduces both that day's working minutes and the month's target, so the hours are not owed.
Flex: A per-date entry that sets that day's working minutes in either direction and leaves the month's target alone, so the difference is compensated on other days of the month.
Reconciliation: The plan's adjustment of the days after today, in fixed increments, to bring the month's balance inside its target band.
Notice: Something the system reports.
Estimate: A task's total planned effort in minutes, the only stored effort value.
Remaining effort: The estimate minus the task's logged minutes.
Completion slot: The five minutes the plan holds for an unfinished task whose remaining effort has reached zero, as a placeholder for the act of completing it.
Concurrent work: More than one task in progress at the same time.
Forecast: The answer to whether a task or project can finish by its effective deadline, with a projected finish, the slack, a risk value, and an explanation.
Slack: The capacity minutes between now and an effective deadline, minus the unallocated effort of the whole dependency closure.
Risk: One of `blocked`, `missed`, `unscheduled`, `tight`, and `safe`, decided in that order of precedence.
Cursor: An opaque position in the change log that a caller passes back to receive what changed since.
Pending operation: A recorded intent waiting for a human's approval, holding the intent's own parameters, a two-digit confirmation code, an expiry, and an attempt count.
Change feed: The ordered record of stored changes that a caller reads forward from a cursor.
Event stream: The server-sent stream that reports the current cursor when it opens, stored changes as they happen, and notices as they are raised.
Export: The portable representation of the planning data: a zip holding one documented JSON document plus an attachments directory.
Backup: A copy of the database file, taken with `VACUUM INTO` or by copying the data directory while no service owner runs.
Purge: The permanent deletion of cancelled and archived records older than the configured age.
